case.title: The Quarry Vote
case.hook: Hi, I’m June Calloway, a geologist (a scientist who studies rocks and the land). A company wants to dig a rock quarry (a big pit where rock is dug out) at the edge of my town, Palmetto Springs. The town votes Thursday. Will you help me weigh it?

notice.head: Public notice · Palmetto Springs Town Council
notice.title: Should we say yes to a rock quarry?
rows: Dig limestone for 20 years to make road rock and building stone.
West of town, beside Cypress Slough (a wetland where herons and wood storks feed), about a mile from the town wells.

stills.alt: An aerial photo: flat brown-green sawgrass on the left, then big square lakes where rock was dug out, with white rock roads between them.
A tall pale yellow wall of limestone rock inside a Florida quarry, under a blue sky.
Tall green sawgrass growing out of bumpy gray limestone rock in a wetland.

Limestone wall in the Brooksville quarry (Suwannee Limestone): RealGatba, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Sawgrass on limestone, Everglades National Park: Moni3, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Palmetto Springs is a made-up town; the photos show real places in Florida like it.
case.question: Should Palmetto Springs say yes to the quarry, and what would make it worth it?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Every choice has two sides: something you gain and something you use up. The quarry is a choice, too.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: load the scale
clues.t: The quarry’s benefits (road rock, jobs, building stone) and its costs (the wetland, the wells, noise and dust) both weigh a lot. Protection strategies made the costs smaller, but not zero.
There are four kinds of protection strategies: conservation, restoration, better technology, and rules. A quarry can use all four.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: the town hall
clues.t: Neighbors see different benefits and costs. Each big cost had a protection strategy to match: restore a wetland nearby, and keep the digging away from the wells.

solve.title: Should Palmetto Springs say yes?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Yes, no problem. A quarry has no environmental cost.
options.why: Check Clue 2. What went on the cost side of the scale?

options.t: No. If a choice has any cost at all, the town should never make it.
options.why: Check Clue 1. Every choice has a cost. Is there a way to make this one smaller?

options.t: Yes, but only with protection strategies. The town gains road rock and jobs, the wetland and wells pay a cost, and strategies like restoring a wetland and keeping away from the wells make that cost smaller.
options.why: Case cracked! You weighed the benefits against the costs and found ways to lower the costs. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

twocol.title: Gained or used up?
todo: Pick one, then drag each card to GAINED or USED UP (or tap a card, then a column).
Sort all three, then answer the question.

chips.miss: Being clean is something you get. Is that gained or used up?
Where does the water go after the shower? Down the drain. Is that gained or used up?
A water heater burns gas or uses electricity. Is that gained or used up?

chips.t: Energy from food for your body
chips.miss: Food gives your body energy. Do you get that or give it up?

chips.t: Bread made from wheat grown on a farm
chips.miss: Once you eat the bread, it’s gone. Is that gained or used up?
The toaster runs on electricity from a power plant. Is that gained or used up?
Getting there fast is a good thing you get. Gained or used up?
The engine burns gas, and then it’s gone. Gained or used up?

chips.t: Some clean air (the car makes exhaust)
chips.miss: Exhaust makes the air a little dirtier. Did the air gain or lose something?

opts.miss: Look at the USED UP column. Is it empty?

opts.t: Something gained AND something used up.

opts.miss: Look at the GAINED column. Is it empty?

twocol.win: Every choice has two sides. The quarry is a choice too. That’s a clue.

scale.afterText: Scientists break a tradeoff into three parts
scale.title: Load the scale
todo: Drag each card to a side of the scale (or tap a card, then a side). Heavy cards (●●●) count more.
Then add the protection strategies and watch the scale.

why.t: The Palmetto Springs quarry. Real rock pits like it, beside the Everglades, supply about half of Florida’s limestone.

weights.t: Rock to fix the town’s roads
weights.miss: Fixing roads is something the town GAINS. Which side is that?
Jobs are something people GAIN. Which side is that?
Building stone is something people GAIN. Which side is that?

weights.t: Part of the wetland dug away for good
weights.miss: The herons and wood storks LOSE their feeding place. Which side is that?

weights.t: A risk to the water in the town wells
weights.miss: Dirty well water would be a LOSS for the town. Which side is that?

weights.t: Noise and dust from big trucks
weights.miss: Noise and dust make the air worse. Which side is that?

strategies.t: The company pays to restore a wetland nearby
strategies.why: Restoration: a fee on every ton of rock pays to bring back wetland somewhere close. Real Florida rock pits pay a fee like this. The wetland here is still gone, so the cost is smaller, but not zero.

strategies.t: A rule: no digging near the town wells
strategies.why: A rule and law: keeping the pit far from the wells lowers the risk to drinking water. It doesn’t remove every risk.

scale.q: The strategies tipped the scale. Is the environmental cost zero now?

opts.t: Yes. The wetland is fine now.
opts.miss: Look at the cost side. Is it empty?

opts.t: No. The costs are smaller, but some of the wetland is still gone.

opts.miss: Look at which side changed when you added the strategies.

scale.credit: Lake Belt rock pits: South Florida Water Management District, Lake Belt Committee (they supply about half of the limestone used in Florida each year; a fee on every ton of rock pays to restore wetlands). Florida mine reclamation: Florida Department of Environmental Protection.
scale.win: Benefits on one side, costs on the other. Protection strategies made the costs smaller, but not zero. That’s a clue.

toolbox.title: Strategy toolbox
todo: Drag each card into its drawer (or tap a card, then a drawer).
Round 2 is the quarry. Then answer the question.

cards.t: Turn off the faucet while you brush your teeth
cards.why: You use less water, so more stays in the aquifer (the water stored in the rock underground).
cards.miss: This uses less of something. Which drawer is about using less?

cards.t: Plant trees and wetland plants around an old mine pit
cards.why: Florida law says land mined for phosphate since 1975 must be fixed up afterward. Some old pits are parks now.
cards.miss: This fixes the land after the digging is done. Which drawer is that?

cards.t: Use solar panels instead of a coal power plant
cards.why: Solar panels make electricity without smoke. It’s a smarter way to do the same job.
cards.miss: This is a new, smarter machine for the same job. Which drawer is that?

cards.t: A law that limits which days people may water their lawns
cards.why: Many Florida towns let people water lawns only on certain days. Everyone has to follow it.
cards.miss: Everyone has to follow this. Which drawer is that?

rounds.title: Strategies for the Palmetto Springs quarry

cards.t: Crush old concrete into road rock, so less new rock is dug
cards.why: Reusing old concrete means the quarry digs less new limestone, so it lasts longer.
cards.miss: This means less new rock gets dug. Which drawer is about using less?

cards.t: Shape finished pits into lakes with plants for birds
cards.why: After digging stops, the pit is reshaped and planted so wildlife can come back.
cards.miss: This happens after the digging is finished. Which drawer is that?

cards.t: Trucks that spray water to keep dust down
cards.why: A spray system is a machine that makes the job cleaner.
cards.miss: This is a machine that does the job better. Which drawer is that?

cards.t: No digging within a mile of the town wells
cards.why: A rule protects drinking water that the whole town shares.
cards.miss: The company has to follow this. Which drawer is that?

toolbox.q: Which kind of strategy fixes damage AFTER the resource is used?

opts.miss: Conservation means using less. Which one fixes things afterward?
Rules stop problems before they start. Which one fixes damage afterward?

toolbox.win: Four kinds of protection strategies, and the quarry can use all of them. That’s a clue.

photos.afterText: None of these makes the environmental cost ZERO
photos.kicker: Look closer · an old Florida quarry
photos.title: What happens to a quarry after the digging?
todo: Tap each number on the photo to read what it is.
Then match the clues to the labels below.

why.t: An old limestone quarry on Key Largo, in the Florida Keys. No one digs here now.

photos.alt: A dark pool of water in an old quarry. Behind it is a low wall of gray rock, with trees and bushes growing along the top under a blue sky.
photos.credit: Quarry, Key Largo, Florida, YourWorldExplorer, via Wikimedia Commons (from Panoramio)

hotspots.label: The gray rock wall
hotspots.t: Limestone made from an old coral reef. This is the rock that was cut out of the ground here.

hotspots.label: The dark water
hotspots.t: Florida’s underground water is close to the surface. When a pit is dug deep enough, water seeps in from the rock and fills it.

hotspots.label: The trees
hotspots.t: Trees and bushes grow right up to the edge. Plants can move back after the digging stops, but it takes many years.

hotspots.label: The flat top of the wall
hotspots.t: This was the ground level before the digging. Everything below it, down past the water, was dug away.

task.q: Match each clue to a label on the photo.
task.win: You read the quarry like a geologist. The rock is gone for good, but nature is slowly moving back in. That’s why the cost is never zero.

items.step: The kind of rock that was dug out
items.evid: The rock wall is limestone that was cut out of the ground.

items.step: What filled the pit from below
items.evid: Underground water seeped in and filled the pit.
Trees and bushes are growing back around the pit.

items.step: Where the ground used to be
items.evid: The top of the wall shows where the ground was before.

townhall.afterText: Six neighbors handed in comment cards
townhall.title: The town hall
todo: Stamp each comment card: Benefit, Cost or Strategy.
Then match each strategy to the cost it lowers, and answer the question.

why.t: A meeting where neighbors share ideas before leaders vote. Listening to everyone helps a town see the whole tradeoff.

comments.t: Our roads are full of potholes. Rock from close by means faster, cheaper repairs.
comments.miss: Fixing roads is something the town gains. Which stamp fits?

comments.t: Wood storks and herons feed in Cypress Slough. Once it’s dug out, that part is gone.
comments.miss: Losing the birds’ feeding place is a loss for the environment. Which stamp fits?

comments.t: Our wells pull drinking water from the same limestone. A pit too close could let pollution in.
comments.miss: Polluted drinking water would be a loss. Which stamp fits?

comments.t: The quarry would hire about 60 people. I could get a job close to home!
comments.miss: A job is something people gain. Which stamp fits?

comments.t: The company could pay to restore a wetland twice as big on land nearby.
comments.miss: This idea lowers a cost. Which stamp fits?
comments.matchMiss: A new wetland helps the birds. Whose card is about the birds?

comments.t: We could make a rule: no digging within a mile of the town wells.
comments.miss: This rule lowers a cost. Which stamp fits?
comments.matchMiss: This rule protects the wells. Whose card is about drinking water?

townhall.matchQ: Now drag each strategy onto the cost it lowers (or tap it, then the cost).
townhall.q: What did the town hall show?

opts.t: Everyone agrees, so there’s nothing to weigh.
opts.miss: Look at the stamps. Did everyone talk about the same side?

opts.t: Neighbors see different benefits and costs, and each big cost has a strategy that can lower it.
Only the benefits matter at a town hall.
opts.miss: Look at the cost cards. Did the town hall ignore them?

townhall.win: Every big cost has a protection strategy to match. That’s your last clue.

tool.name: Water meter
tool.teaser: Run a shower, a dripping faucet and a lawn sprinkler, and read how many gallons each one uses.
tool.done: You read the water meter like a pro. A water meter sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.t: A counter on the pipe that brings water to a home. It adds up every gallon used, so families and towns can see where their water goes.

watermeter.title: Where does a home’s water go?
todo: Tap each part of the meter to learn it.
Run all four ways of using water and watch the meter count.
Compare the bars, then answer the question.

parts.label: The counter
parts.t: The numbers add up every gallon that has gone through the pipe. They only go up.

parts.label: The sweep hand
parts.t: The big red hand goes around once for every 10 gallons on many home meters, so you can see small amounts.

parts.label: The leak triangle
parts.t: This little triangle spins whenever any water is flowing, even a tiny drip. If it spins when everything is off, there’s a leak.

uses.name: A 10-minute shower
uses.note: A new shower head can use up to 2.5 gallons every minute, so 10 minutes is about 25 gallons.

uses.name: A 5-minute shower
uses.note: Half the time, about half the water (about 12 or 13 gallons). That’s conservation.

uses.name: A dripping faucet for a whole day
uses.note: One drip every second adds up to about 8 gallons a day, and more than 3,000 gallons a year. Watch the leak triangle spin.

uses.name: Watering the lawn once
uses.note: A typical Florida yard uses about 1,000 gallons or more each time the sprinklers run.

q.q: Which change would save the MOST water in one week?

opts.why: That saves about 12 gallons a shower, or about 85 gallons in a week. Good, but look at the longest bar.
That saves about 8 gallons a day, or about 56 in a week. Good, but look at the longest bar.

opts.t: Watering the lawn one less time each week
opts.why: Right! Skipping one watering saves about 1,000 gallons, more than all the others together. That’s why Florida towns limit which days people may water lawns.

q1.B: Those are map words from 15.02. Which three parts did the scale have?

q2.B: Drip irrigation saves water. Does that lower a cost or add one?

q3.A: Coal makes smoke. Solar farms cover land. Are those the same cost?
q3.C: Think about Load the scale. Was any cost ever zero?

cer-4.label: your reasoning
cer-4.re: because|so |this shows|that shows|this means|that means|which means|proves|since

ans-1: Pick the one you understand best: gas cars, solar farms, phosphate mining or irrigation farms.
Write three sentences: what people gain, what the environment loses, what lowers the cost.
Try: The benefit of ___ is ___. The environmental cost is ___. One protection strategy is ___.
ans-3: What happened to the cost side of the scale when you added a strategy?
Think of a Florida example from the toolbox.
Try: Protection strategies matter because ___. For example, ___ lowers the cost by ___.
cer-4: First decide: should Florida ALWAYS pick what’s best for the environment, no matter what?
Think about the roads and the wetland in Palmetto Springs.
Try: I ___ because ___. One piece of evidence is ___. Another is ___.

planner.title: Your claim and two pieces of evidence

rows.label: 2. Pick two pieces of evidence from the lesson
options: Every choice has two sides: something gained and something used up.
The quarry gives the town road rock and jobs, but it costs part of the wetland.

Restoring a wetland nearby and keeping away from the wells lowered the biggest costs.

planner.note: Tap your side and two facts. Then write your reasoning in your own words.

welcome.label: Welcome · the quarry vote
welcome.script: Hi! I’m June Calloway, and I’m a geologist. That means I study rocks and the land. I work in Palmetto Springs, a little Florida town. A company wants to dig a rock quarry right next to our wetland. The quarry would bring road rock and jobs. But what would we lose? The town votes on Thursday. Help me weigh it.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · gained or used up? (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Let’s start small. Pick something you might do in the morning, like a shower or a car ride. Then sort each card. Is it something you gained, or something you used up? Sort all three. Then write about something you really did today.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Act out “tradeoff” by trading a pencil for an eraser; hold out two hands like a scale for “benefit” and “environmental cost”.

part1.label: Part 1 · load the scale (Clue 2)
part1.script: Here’s our quarry on a balance scale. Drag each card to the benefit side or the cost side. Heavy cards count more, so watch the scale tip. When every card is on, add the protection strategies. What happens to the cost side? Does it ever reach zero?

part2.label: Part 2 · strategy toolbox (Clue 3)
part2.script: A good town needs a whole toolbox of strategies. Drop each card into its drawer: using less, fixing damage afterward, a smarter machine, or a rule everyone follows. Round two is our quarry. After that, I’ll show you a real old quarry in the Florida Keys.

explore.label: Part 4 · the town hall (Clue 4)
explore.script: Welcome to the town hall! Six neighbors brought comment cards. Read each one and stamp it: a benefit, a cost, or a protection strategy. Then match each strategy to the cost it lowers. Listen to everyone. That’s how a town sees the whole tradeoff.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: should Palmetto Springs say yes to the quarry, and what would make it worth it? Then answer two questions, weigh one Florida tradeoff in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says Florida should always pick what’s best for the environment, no matter what. Hmm. Think about the roads and the wetland in Palmetto Springs. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease 16.02 (compare several solutions and improve one, like an engineer).
closing.script: Case closed! You weighed the benefits and the costs, and you found strategies to make the costs smaller. That’s exactly what a good town does. Next time, we’ll think like engineers: compare a few different solutions, pick the best one, and make it even better.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain what we gain and what we lose when we use a resource?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: The quarry gives the town road rock, but it costs part of the wetland.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “road rock”, “costs” and “wetland”. Those words tell the benefit and the cost. Small words like “the” and “but” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
